items.readable_text:
Content:
It's possible to write exponential functions in many different, equivalent forms. Depending on the situation, we may prefer one form over another if it displays characteristics we're interested in more clearly.

Content:
For example, consider the following exponential function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=35\cdot(1.4)^{x+1}]

Content:
It's possible to express this function in a variety of different forms using the laws of exponents. Let's go through some of the most common:

Content:
- We can write the function [MATH: f] in an equivalent form with [MATH: x] only in the exponent using the product rule in reverse.
[MATH: f(x)|= 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{x + 1}; = 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{x} ⋅ (1.4)^{1}; = 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{x} ⋅ 1.4; = 35 ⋅ 1.4 ⋅ (1.4)^{x}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x}]
- Similarly, we can write the function [MATH: f] in an equivalent form with [MATH: (x-1)] in the exponent as follows:
[MATH: f(x)|= 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1 + 1}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1} ⋅ (1.4)^{1}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1} ⋅ 1.4; = 49 ⋅ 1.4 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1}; = 68.6 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1}]

Content:
Therefore, our function [MATH: f] has the following equivalent forms:

Content:
- [MATH: f(x) = 35\cdot(1.4)^{x+1}]
- [MATH: f(x) = 49 \cdot (1.4)^x]
- [MATH: f(x) = 68.6 \cdot (1.4)^{x-1}]

Content:
Please note that exponential functions have many equivalent forms. For the function [MATH: f] here, this is only three of them.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
It's possible to write exponential functions in many different, equivalent forms. Depending on the situation, we may prefer one form over another if it displays characteristics we're interested in more clearly.

Content:
For example, consider the following exponential function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=35\cdot(1.4)^{x+1}]

Content:
It's possible to express this function in a variety of different forms using the laws of exponents. Let's go through some of the most common:

Content:
- We can write the function [MATH: f] in an equivalent form with [MATH: x] only in the exponent using the product rule in reverse.
[MATH: f(x)|= 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{x + 1}; = 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{x} ⋅ (1.4)^{1}; = 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{x} ⋅ 1.4; = 35 ⋅ 1.4 ⋅ (1.4)^{x}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x}]
- Similarly, we can write the function [MATH: f] in an equivalent form with [MATH: (x-1)] in the exponent as follows:
[MATH: f(x)|= 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1 + 1}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1} ⋅ (1.4)^{1}; = 49 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1} ⋅ 1.4; = 49 ⋅ 1.4 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1}; = 68.6 ⋅ (1.4)^{x − 1}]

Content:
Therefore, our function [MATH: f] has the following equivalent forms:

Content:
- [MATH: f(x) = 35\cdot(1.4)^{x+1}]
- [MATH: f(x) = 49 \cdot (1.4)^x]
- [MATH: f(x) = 68.6 \cdot (1.4)^{x-1}]

Content:
Please note that exponential functions have many equivalent forms. For the function [MATH: f] here, this is only three of them.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Identifying a Form Displaying the Y-Intercept

Content:
As we saw, the function [MATH: f] defined earlier has the following equivalent forms:

Content:
- [MATH: f(x) = 35\cdot(1.4)^{x+1}]
- [MATH: f(x) = 49 \cdot (1.4)^x]
- [MATH: f(x) = 68.6 \cdot (1.4)^{x-1}]

Content:
The coefficients [MATH: 35, 49,] and [MATH: 68.6] all correspond to certain characteristics of the function. We can identify which characteristic a coefficient corresponds to by evaluating the function at certain points.

Content:
For example, the [MATH: y]-intercept is a characteristic of the curve [MATH: y=f(x),] and its value corresponds to [MATH: f(0).] We can determine the [MATH: y]-intercept by finding [MATH: f(0)] using any of the forms given above.

Content:
Evaluating [MATH: f(0)] using the first form, we get
[MATH: f(0)|= 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{x + 1}; = 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{0 + 1}; = 35 ⋅ (1.4)^{1}; = 35 ⋅ 1.4; = 49.]
Notice that this number [MATH: 49] appears as a coefficient in the second form.

Content:
Therefore, we say that the equivalent form [MATH: f(x) = 49 \cdot (1.4)^x] displays the [MATH: y]-intercept as a coefficient.

Item 3 — Tutorial: Identifying a Form Displaying a Function Value

Content:
- [MATH: f(x) = 35\cdot(1.4)^{x+1}]
- [MATH: f(x) = 49 \cdot (1.4)^x]
- [MATH: f(x) = 68.6 \cdot (1.4)^{x-1}]
